strengths: The common construction for forests and ReLU networks is interpretable and relevant to researchers studying probabilistic prediction and OOD behavior. Gaussian decay plus a positive background term provides a transparent mechanism for reverting toward class priors without OOD training examples.

The evaluation spans six synthetic problems, 45 OpenML datasets, and vision benchmarks. Repeated simulations, comparisons against known posteriors, and comparisons of Euclidean and geodesic distances provide useful empirical insights.

Table 1 reports an encouraging tradeoff: CIFAR-10 MCE decreases from 0.13 to 0.02 while accuracy changes from 83.70% to 83.60%, and noise-detection AUROC improves from 0.71 to 0.98. The discussion acknowledges limitations on near-OOD data.
weaknesses: Required: Theorem 1 is false as stated, invalidating a central advertised guarantee. Consider a uniform density on [0,1], odd m, h=1/m, n=m², midpoint kernel centers, and Gaussian standard deviation σ=h/2. At x=1/2, Eq. (5) converges to 2/√(2π)≈0.798 rather than 1, although the stated conditions hold. The nearest-kernel restriction invalidates the normalization argument in Eqs. (23)–(24). Correct the estimator and proof, or withdraw the density-consistency claim and independently justify narrower claims. The stated multidimensional uniform convergence also requires substantially more justification than the one-dimensional nh→∞ calculation.

Required: Correct the probabilistic interpretation. ReLU logits are piecewise affine, but they are not class-conditional densities; tree leaf class frequencies estimate posteriors. Equation (5) generally does not integrate to one because each Gaussian contributes only on its selection region, and the positive constant added in Eq. (6) gives an infinite integral over R^d. Equation (7) can still define class probabilities, but this does not establish the claimed density model.

Required: Corollary 3 does not follow from Theorems 1–2. Convergence as an input recedes to infinity for fixed sample size does not establish uniform convergence over inputs as sample size increases. Moreover, Eq. (1) demands class priors throughout the low-density region outside S; even a consistent density estimator with vanishing bias would instead recover the conditional posterior at fixed points there with positive marginal density. Define S precisely and establish a compatible convergence claim. The application of Theorem 2 to geodesic distance also needs correction: Eq. (18) lies in [0,1], so its distance cannot approach infinity.

Required: The connection between the idealized theory and fitted models is not established. Appendix A uses data-independent kernel parameters, whereas the proposed method estimates parameters and partitions from training data. Corollaries 4–5 do not establish the required partition geometry and occupancy conditions; universal approximation alone does not imply shrinking cells with sufficient observations. Supply valid arguments for a specified algorithm, or explicitly restrict the guarantees to an idealized construction.

Required: Distinguish OOD prior reversion from statistical calibration. OCE in Eq. (19) measures agreement with the maximum training prior without using OOD outcomes; with unequal priors, even different probability vectors can attain zero OCE. Its interpretation requires explicit assumptions. Claims of calibration throughout the feature space also exceed the experiments: tabular OOD inputs are generated on hyperspheres, while Table 1 shows CIFAR-100 AUROC decreasing from 0.78 to 0.69 and SVHN FPR@95 worsening from 0.74 to 0.81. Narrow the claims to the demonstrated behavior or provide additional supporting evidence.

Required: Resolve discrepancies that prevent reproducing the evaluated method. Equations (10)–(11) fit Gaussians using within-polytope samples, whereas Algorithm 1, line 17, specifies similarity-weighted MLE. These are different estimators, and weighting across polytopes need not preserve the claimed center and bandwidth conditions. Specify the search range and objective for k, explain how the fully connected activation-path construction applies to ResNet-20, and clarify whether FPR@95 uses 95% precision, as written, or 95% true-positive rate.

Optional: Temperature scaling would strengthen comparisons with accuracy-preserving calibration. Proper scoring rules such as NLL or Brier score, uncertainty estimates for Table 1, ablations of the background term and similarity weighting, and runtime/memory measurements would make the empirical findings more informative.
